en.title: Nolan and Park Chan-wook Unpack The Odyssey's Magic and Myth
en.summary: Two visionary directors, Christopher Nolan and Park Chan-wook, recently sat down for a captivating conversation about Nolan's blockbuster hit, 'The Odyssey.' They delved into the film's unique storytelling, bold techniques, and the enduring power of epic narratives.
en.body:
The global phenomenon that is **Christopher Nolan**'s **The Odyssey** continues to captivate audiences, and now, the acclaimed director has shared insights into its creation with none other than **Park Chan-wook**, the visionary behind **Oldboy** and **The Handmaiden**.

In a special Masters Talk event, the two filmmakers engaged in a deep dive into Nolan's latest epic. While promoting his film, Nolan expressed his profound admiration for Park's work, stating, "Ever since I saw **Memento**, I have been a huge fan of yours. As movies get bigger, it’s rare and incredibly difficult for them to get better, but you’ve managed to achieve that throughout film history."

Park reciprocated the admiration, highlighting specific elements of **The Odyssey** that resonated with him. He pointed to the film's masterful bookending, particularly the iconic Trojan horse sequence, and the innovative integration of sound design, such as the unique pluck of Odysseus' bowstring woven into the musical score. Park also touched upon memorable moments of violence within the film and the director's choice to omit the traditional pantheon of gods, opting instead for a more grounded, humanistic approach to the ancient myth.

## A Shared Vision for Epic Storytelling

Nolan, in turn, spoke about the challenging yet exhilarating process of bringing **The Odyssey** to life. The film, shot on two million feet of IMAX film over 91 days, aimed to capture the grandeur and visceral impact of Homer's timeless tale. Park's appreciation for Nolan's meticulous approach was evident, especially when he recalled a conversation with **Robert Downey Jr.** about filming **Oppenheimer**. Downey Jr. had described the intense experience of having Nolan's IMAX camera placed directly in front of his face, a testament to the director's commitment to immersive filmmaking.

"Coming from you, that means a lot," Nolan responded to Park's praise. "Other than my immense respect for you and your work, it is a thrilling thing to hear that from a fellow director who understands the process so well."

## Echoes of Ancient Myths in Modern Cinema

The conversation also touched upon the enduring appeal of **The Odyssey** itself and how modern filmmakers can reinterpret its themes for contemporary audiences. Nolan’s film, a critical and commercial success, has resonated with viewers worldwide, proving that epic journeys and tales of human resilience remain as compelling as ever. The discussion between Nolan and Park underscores the universal language of cinema and the shared passion these directors have for crafting unforgettable cinematic experiences.

Park's insights into the film's structure and sound design reveal a keen eye for directorial craft, while Nolan's responses highlight his dedication to pushing the boundaries of filmmaking technology and narrative. This exchange offers fans a deeper appreciation for the artistry behind one of the year's biggest films.

## Looking Ahead

Details regarding any future collaborations or projects stemming from this discussion have not yet been announced, but the conversation itself serves as a powerful reminder of the collaborative and inspiring nature of filmmaking at its highest level.

content_raw: As Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey sets a career record for his highest-grossing film at $1.1 billion, the epic is still rolling out in countries across the world. Another week, and another great conversation has emerged from his tour through Asia. This time, Oldboy and No Other Choice director Park Chan-wook spoke with Nolan about the film as the two shared a mutual admiration for the other’s talents. Park specifically discusses his favorite aspects of the film––the bookending of the Trojan horse, the invention and integration of the sound of Odysseus’ bow-plucking into the score, a memorable moment of violence––as well touching on the title card, the lack of gods, and more. Check out an English translation of the transcription below, edited for clarity, followed by the complete video. Park Chan-wook: Welcome to Korea. Promoting a movie after finishing it is an exhausting process. While I love every step of being a film director, this is the one part I’d like to avoid if possible. How about you? Christopher Nolan: I feel the exact same way. Ever since I saw Memento , I have been a huge fan of yours. As movies get bigger, it’s rare and incredibly difficult for them to get better, but you’ve managed to achieve that throughout film history. Well, thank you. Coming from you, that means a lot. Other than my immense respect for you and your work, it is a thrilling thing to hear that from a fellow director who understands the process so well. I still vividly remember when I was filming The Sympathizer and met Robert Downey Jr. He talked about his experience on Oppenheimer and how exhilarating it was working with you—specifically having your IMAX camera placed right in front of his face. I can still see the expression on his face when he described it. It’s a very large camera and it makes a lot of noise. When you put it right in an actor’s face, they fully understand that all attention is on them and that they have to truly experience the moment for real. Working with Robert on that film—as you know from working with him yourself—was a tremendous thrill to work with a great like him. Speaking of The Odyssey , I was completely captivated right from the opening scene. The wooden horse resting in the sea, the Trojan knights riding towards it… that opening was so beautiful and mesmerizing that I found myself wishing those shots were much longer—maybe even 10 minutes long—because of how deeply pulled in I was. Thank you. It’s tremendous to hear that. That opening image was something I held in my head for a long time—for about 20 years: “How would I approach the Trojan horse? How would I do that?” I became really fascinated by this idea of using the horse not the way it’s traditionally represented, with wheels and easily brought into the city.
